relationship: God amid a divine assembly
rationale: God stands in an assembly of gods and judges in their midst. Psalm 88 describes God glorified in the council of holy ones and fearsome above those around Him. relationship: Justice for the fatherless and vulnerable

relationship: Zebah and Zalmunna as named defeated kings

relationship: Storm and pursuit in a prayer against enemies

relationship: Judgment followed by seeking God
rationale: Psalm 82 asks that faces be filled with dishonor and says they will seek the Lord's name. Psalm 77 recalls people seeking God and remembering their helper when He was killing them. relationship: Enemies brought to shame and trouble

relationship: Enemies recognizing God's worldwide rule

relationship: The face of God's anointed in prayer

relationship: Choosing hardship with God over the pleasures of sin
rationale: The psalmist chooses being cast aside in God's house rather than dwelling in sinners' tents. relationship: Good things not withheld from those devoted to God
rationale: Psalm 83 says God will not deprive those walking in innocence of good things. relationship: A blessing on the person who hopes in the Lord

relationship: The Lord turning back captivity
rationale: Psalm 84 remembers the Lord turning back Jacob's captivity and taking pleasure in His land. Psalm 125 opens with the Lord turning back Zion's captivity and the people's comfort. relationship: Forgiven lawlessness and covered sins
rationale: Psalm 84 thanks God for forgiving His people's acts of lawlessness and covering all their sins. Psalm 31 blesses those whose lawless deeds were forgiven and whose sins were covered. The paired forgiveness and covering formulation corresponds directly, with communal thanksgiving and beatitude as different forms.

relationship: Divine anger turned away
rationale: Psalm 84 recalls God stopping His wrath and turning away His fury. Isaiah's song thanks the Lord after His anger and says He turned away His wrath and showed mercy. Both describe an experienced reversal of divine anger as grounds for thankful speech.

relationship: Restoration sought in the presence of divine anger
rationale: The source asks God to turn the people back and turn His fury away. Lamentations asks the Lord to turn them back, renew their days, and confronts their rejection and His great anger. relationship: Divine anger questioned or denied as everlasting
rationale: Psalm 84 asks whether God will remain angry for ever and extend wrath through generations. Psalm 102 says He will not be angry to the end or maintain anger for ever. The common question of anger's duration receives a direct assurance in the target, rather than the source already asserting that assurance.

relationship: God turning back to give life
rationale: The source anticipates God turning back and giving the people life, followed by their rejoicing. The turning and life-giving action connects communal hope with an individual's recollection and hope.

relationship: Mercy and salvation requested together
rationale: Psalm 84 asks the Lord to show His mercy and give His salvation. Psalm 118 asks that His mercy and salvation come to the speaker according to His saying. Both petitions explicitly pair mercy and salvation, while the second adds the ground of God's spoken promise.

relationship: Listening for what God speaks within
rationale: The psalmist will hear what the Lord God speaks within him, expecting peace for God's people. relationship: Divine glory dwelling among God's people
rationale: Psalm 84 connects salvation's nearness with glory dwelling in the land. Zechariah promises that the Lord will be a fiery wall around Jerusalem and glory in her midst. Divine glory residing among the people is shared, with the land and the specifically measured city as distinct settings.

relationship: Heaven and earth pictured through righteous growth

relationship: Divine provision and the land's fruit
rationale: The source expects the Lord to give goodness and the land to give its fruit. relationship: Personified virtues going before God

relationship: God's response to those who call on Him

relationship: Calling on God in a day of affliction

relationship: The Lord incomparable among gods

relationship: All nations coming to worship the Lord

rationale: Psalm 85 asks for guidance in God's way and anticipates walking in His truth. Psalm 24 asks God to show His ways, teach His paths, and guide the speaker into His truth. rationale: Psalm 85 promises thanksgiving to the Lord with all the heart and enduring glorification of His name. relationship: The soul rescued from Hades
rationale: Psalm 85 says God's great mercy delivered the speaker's soul from lowest Hades. Psalm 29 thanks the Lord for bringing the soul up from Hades and saving the speaker from descent into a pit. relationship: Strong adversaries seeking the soul without regard for God
rationale: Psalm 85 says an assembly of strong men sought the speaker's soul and did not set God before them. relationship: The confession of divine compassion and mercy
rationale: Psalm 85 addresses the Lord as compassionate, merciful, long-suffering, abundant in mercy and true. relationship: The servant who is a maidservant's son
rationale: Psalm 85 asks might and salvation for God's servant, the son of His maidservant. relationship: Divine comfort and the shame of enemies

relationship: God's city and its foundation

relationship: Zion or Jerusalem described as mother

relationship: Zion and a register of its people

relationship: Dwelling in a city characterized by rejoicing

relationship: The heading concerning Maeleth
rationale: Both headings include 'concerning Maeleth' and a notice of understanding. Psalm 87 additionally has the sons of Korah, answering and Heman the Israelite, whereas Psalm 52 names David. The unusual shared heading is retained without assigning Maeleth an unexpressed musical meaning or identifying the authors.

relationship: Crying to God by day and night
rationale: Psalm 87 addresses the God of salvation and describes crying by day and before Him by night. Psalm 21 likewise describes crying by day and night but complains that God will not hear. relationship: A suffering life approaching death and Hades
rationale: The psalmist's life drew near Hades as his soul filled with evils. Elihu describes a sick person's soul drawing near death and his life being in Hades. relationship: Being counted with those descending into a pit

relationship: Dark places associated with the dead

relationship: God's overwhelming surges upon the speaker

relationship: Estrangement from acquaintances and close relations

relationship: Hands spread toward God in distress

The explicit bodily gesture toward God connects the distressed prayers; the accompanying images remain different.

relationship: The dead and the possibility of thanksgiving
rationale: The source asks about wonders for the dead and whether physicians will raise them to give thanks. rationale: Psalm 87 asks whether anyone will recount God's mercy in a grave or His truth in destruction. Psalm 6 says no one in death remembers God and asks who will give thanks in Hades. relationship: Death's land depicted as darkness
rationale: Psalm 87 asks whether God's wonders and righteousness will be known in darkness and a forgotten land. relationship: Divine truth enduring with a heavenly reference

relationship: Divine power defeating enemies

relationship: God's ownership and founding of the world
rationale: Psalm 88 calls heaven, earth and the inhabited world's fullness God's and says He founded them. Psalm 23 likewise declares the earth and its fullness the Lord's and says He founded it. rationale: Psalm 88 names Tabor and Hermon exulting in God's name after mentioning His creation of the north and seas. Psalm 97 summons mountains to exult together, alongside clapping rivers. The divine throne and its moral basis correspond, while mercy and truth proceeding before God belong to the source's additional clause.

relationship: Blessing and the light of God's face
rationale: The psalm blesses the people and says they will walk in the light of the Lord's face. The priestly blessing asks the Lord to make His face shine upon the recipient and lift His face toward him. The particular connection of divine facial light and blessing is shared, with communal walking and priestly petition as different expressions.

relationship: Joy in God's name
rationale: Psalm 88 anticipates people exulting in God's name throughout the day. Psalm 32 says the community's heart will rejoice in Him because it hoped in His holy name. Both join communal joy with God's name, while the target expressly gives hope as the reason and the source also mentions being raised in righteousness.

relationship: Strength and a horn raised by God
rationale: Psalm 88 names God the boast of the people's power and expects their horn to be raised by His favor. Hannah's song says God gives strength to the kings and will raise the horn of His anointed. The paired divine strength and raised horn are shared, with the community and the expressly royal recipients distinguished.

relationship: God as Israel's King
rationale: The psalm places support with the Lord and the Holy One of Israel, our King. Isaiah introduces God as Israel's King and rescuer before declaring His uniqueness. The particular attribution of Israel's kingship to God supports the link; Isaiah 44:6 does not itself repeat the Holy One designation.

relationship: David raised from among the people to royal service
rationale: The source recalls a vision in which God raised a chosen one from His people, identified as David in the following unit. Nathan's message recalls God taking His servant David from the sheepfold to lead Israel; its surrounding account calls the message a vision. Both describe David's elevation by God, with the sheepfold detail supplied only by Samuel.

relationship: David's anointing with oil
rationale: The divine speech says God found David His servant and anointed him with holy oil. Samuel narrates the Lord identifying the youngest son and commanding his anointing, then Samuel taking the horn of oil and anointing him. The named David and actual oil-anointing correspond, with God as authorizer and Samuel as executor distinguished.

relationship: Divine strength and supporting hand
rationale: God promises His supporting hand and strengthening arm to David. In Isaiah He tells Israel not to fear and says He strengthened, helped and secured the addressee with His righteous right hand. Strength and divine bodily support connect the assurances, while David and Israel, and promised and stated accomplished help, remain distinct.

relationship: Protection from lawless harm in the Davidic promise
rationale: Psalm 88 promises that no son of lawlessness will go on to harm David. Nathan's message promises a place for Israel and says no unjust man will again humble the people. Both belong to promises of protection in the Davidic setting, but the psalm's royal individual and Samuel's people Israel are different recipients.

relationship: David's enemies removed before him
rationale: Psalm 88 promises that God will cut down David's enemies before him and put his haters to flight. Nathan's message recalls God's presence with David and destruction of his enemies before him. The named beneficiary and enemies removed before him connect promise and retrospective declaration without erasing the tense difference.

relationship: The raising of David's horn
rationale: God promises David His truth and mercy and says his horn will be raised in His name. Psalm 131 says God will make a horn sprout for David and prepared a lamp for His anointed. The divine raising or growth of David's horn is a specific royal image, while the source's name and the target's lamp remain different accompanying elements.

relationship: Royal reach expressed through sea and river
rationale: Psalm 88 says God will set the king's hand in the sea and his right hand in rivers. Psalm 71 describes the king ruling from sea to sea and from the river to the inhabited world's extremities. The waters express royal reach in both, with David's promise and the poem headed for Solomon kept in their respective settings.

relationship: God as Father in a royal promise
rationale: Psalm 88 anticipates the king calling God his Father, God and supporter of salvation. Nathan's oracle promises that God will be a father to David's offspring and that the offspring will be His son. The royal father-son relationship is explicit in both, while David's role in the psalm and the promised offspring in Samuel are not collapsed into one immediate addressee.

relationship: Firstborn status associated with preeminence
rationale: Psalm 88 promises to make the king firstborn and high among earth's kings. Colossians calls the Son firstborn of all creation and firstborn from the dead so that He may have preeminence in everything. The firstborn and preeminence pattern is comparable, while royal rank, creation and resurrection are distinct scopes and an identity claim is not inferred from the term alone.

relationship: Mercy retained and the royal promise made secure
rationale: God promises to keep mercy for the king for ever and calls His covenant faithful to him. Nathan's oracle promises that mercy will not be withdrawn and that the house, kingdom and throne will be made secure for ever. The continued mercy and secure royal promise connect the passages, without inserting a name for the target's unnamed removed predecessors.

relationship: An enduring dynasty and throne
rationale: Psalm 88 promises the king's seed for an age of an age and his throne like heaven's days. Samuel promises the house and kingdom made secure for ever and the throne established for ever. The enduring descendants or house and throne correspond, while the heaven-days comparison belongs expressly to the psalm.

relationship: Royal sons and keeping God's ways
rationale: The source introduces the condition that the king's sons abandon God's law and judgments, leading to discipline in the following units. David's charge to Solomon joins keeping the Lord's commands with the promise concerning sons guarding their ways and continuing on Israel's throne. Both connect the royal descendants with obedience, without equating the distinct consequences stated in their contexts.

relationship: Royal descendants forsaking commandments
rationale: Psalm 88 continues the condition of descendants profaning ordinances and failing to keep commandments. God's warning to Solomon names him and his children turning away and not keeping commandments, followed by judgment on Israel and the house. The stated failure of royal descendants is comparable; the collective judgment in Kings is not substituted for the psalm's subsequent rod and scourges.

relationship: Royal wrongdoing disciplined with a rod
rationale: Psalm 88 promises to visit the sons' lawless acts with a rod and sins with scourges. Nathan's oracle promises fatherly correction of the royal offspring's wrongdoing with a rod of men and afflictions of human beings. The particular rod of discipline within the royal promise is shared, while scourges and afflictions remain the texts' different wording.

relationship: Mercy not withdrawn after royal discipline
rationale: After its threat of discipline, Psalm 88 promises not to scatter mercy away from the king or act unjustly in truth. Samuel likewise follows the disciplinary promise with assurance that God's mercy will not be withdrawn. The conjunction of correction and retained mercy is specific; the target's unnamed removed predecessors are not silently named.

relationship: God's spoken word not set aside
rationale: The psalm promises that God will not profane His covenant or set aside what goes out through His lips. Balaam's oracle asks whether God speaks without doing or says without abiding by it. The reliability of divine speech is shared; Numbers's preceding descriptions of being led astray and threatened are not replaced with a different familiar wording.

relationship: God's truthful oath to David
rationale: God says He once swore by His holiness and will not lie to David. Psalm 131 says the Lord swore truth to David and will not annul it, then mentions a descendant on his throne. The named recipient, oath and truthfulness directly correspond, with holiness and non-annulment as their respective additional expressions.

relationship: Royal endurance measured with the sun
rationale: Psalm 88 promises enduring royal seed and a throne like the sun before God. Psalm 71 says the king will remain beside the sun and before the moon through generations. Solar endurance within royal language is shared, while a throne and the royal figure are the differently expressed subjects.

relationship: The moon's order and enduring divine commitment
rationale: Psalm 88 compares the promised royal endurance to the moon established for ever and a faithful heavenly witness. Jeremiah names God's ordering of sun, moon and stars and says Israel's family would cease being a nation if those laws ceased. Celestial stability supports an enduring commitment in both, with David's line and Israel's national existence distinguished.

relationship: same-chapter contrast between anointing and rejection
rationale: The lament says God put off His anointed, whereas the earlier divine speech names David and says God anointed him with holy oil. The return to the anointed makes the lament's tension with the recalled favor explicit, without identifying the unnamed lamented king as the historical David.

relationship: same-chapter tension over the covenant
rationale: The lament says God overturned His servant's covenant, after the promise that He would not profane His covenant or set aside His words. This direct covenant contrast structures the complaint. The source's accompanying profaned consecrated thing is preserved as stated rather than renamed a crown.

relationship: God removing protective fences
rationale: Psalm 88 laments God tearing down the king's fences and making his fortifications cowardice. Psalm 79 asks why God tore down the vine's fence, exposing it to those passing along the road. The removal of protection under divine agency is shared, with king and national vine as different images and cowardice not changed into ruins.

relationship: Road travelers taking from an exposed possession
rationale: Psalm 88 says all who travel the road plundered the king. Psalm 79 says everyone traveling the road harvests the vine after its fence was removed. The distinctive road-passers taking from what has been exposed connects the images, while plundering a king and harvesting the national vine remain distinct actions.

relationship: same-chapter reversal concerning the king's enemies
rationale: The lament says God raised the enemies' right hand and gladdened them. Earlier He promised to cut the king's enemies down and put his haters to flight. Their rise and joy reverse the expected defeat within the poem's own promise-and-lament sequence.

relationship: God's support absent in warfare
rationale: Psalm 88 says God turned back the help of the king's sword and did not support him in war. Psalm 43 laments divine rejection and shame and says God will not go out with the forces. Both describe military weakness through absent divine accompaniment, with a royal individual and communal forces, and past and future expression, distinguished.

relationship: same-chapter contrast over the throne
rationale: The lament says God dashed the king's throne to the ground, whereas His earlier promise was to build David's throne through generations. The opposed treatment of the throne supplies a direct internal contrast. This connection does not attempt to explain the source's separate statement about removal from purification.

relationship: Shortened royal days contrasted with granted length of life
rationale: Psalm 88 laments the shortening of the king's days and the pouring of shame upon him. Psalm 20 says the king asked for life and received length of days for an age of an age. The treatment of royal lifespan forms a particular contrast without identifying the two unnamed kings or changing shame into a different royal attribute.

relationship: The question of enduring wrath like fire
rationale: Both passages ask 'How long' and describe divine wrath or jealous anger burning like fire. Psalm 88 asks whether God will turn away to the end, while Psalm 78 questions anger to the end. The extended fire-and-duration complaint is shared in royal and communal laments.

relationship: A plea to remember fragile human existence
rationale: Psalm 88 asks God to remember what the speaker's existence is before questioning whether all humans were created in vain. Job likewise asks God to remember that his life is a breath and speaks of passing good things. Both address human transience to God through a remembrance plea; the psalm's creation question remains a question.

relationship: Human inability to control death
rationale: The psalm asks who will live without seeing death and deliver his soul from Hades' hand. Ecclesiastes denies human authority over the spirit and over the day of death. Both confront human inability to secure life against death; neither comparison turns that human limitation into a denial of God's power to rescue.

relationship: same-chapter appeal back to the oath to David
rationale: The closing question about ancient mercies invokes what God swore to David in truth. The opening divine speech explicitly records His oath to David His servant alongside the covenant with His chosen ones. The later appeal returns to that particular oath as the ground for questioning the present experience.

relationship: Bearing reproach associated with God
rationale: Psalm 88 asks God to remember His servants' reproach borne by the speaker from many nations. Psalm 68 says reproaches of those reproaching God fell upon the speaker. Both describe personally bearing reproach within a relationship to God, with the servants' reproach and reproach aimed at God kept as different objects.

relationship: An enduring blessing closed by repeated assent
rationale: Psalm 88 closes with blessing the Lord for ever and twice saying 'May it be.' Psalm 40 likewise closes by blessing the Lord, Israel's God, from age to age and repeating 'May it be.' The extended closing doxology and doubled assent form a particular literary correspondence.
